items.t: Hong Kong Stocks Sink 1.89% As Hang Seng Enters Bear Market
sum: Hong Kong stocks extended their losses on Friday, with the benchmark Hang Seng Index (HSI) falling 1.89% to its lowest closing level in more than a year as concerns over artificial intelligence (AI) spending and semiconductor industry weakness triggered another broad sell-off.

The HSI dropped 430.82 points to 22,410.80, marking its fourth consecutive session of losses and its lowest close since April 30, 2025. The index also briefly fell as much as 2.2% during the session, bringing its decline from the Jan 29 peak to 20%, the threshold for a bear market.

Technology stocks bore the brunt of the selling, with the Hang Seng Tech Index plunging 3.78% to 3,511.14. The Hang Seng China Enterprises Index, which tracks mainland Chinese companies listed in Hong Kong, fell 1.77% to 7,554.37.
Investor concerns over the sustainability of AI investment weighed on technology and semiconductor counters, extending a regional sell-off following sharp losses on Wall Street.

NetEase was among the biggest drags, plunging 17.6% after reporting a quarterly revenue decline. Tencent Holdings fell 1.26% to HK$344, its lowest level in more than two years, amid concerns over the impact of AI-related spending on margins.
Other notable decliners included battery maker CATL, which fell 4.23%, and lidar manufacturer Hesai, down 5.67%. Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing also lost more than 3%.
Alibaba-W bucked the broader weakness, rising 3.48% following its earnings announcement.

items.t: Hong Kong Stock Exchange: Hang Seng Index Slides to 22,410.80 Amid US-Iran Negotiations
sum: Hong Kong's benchmark posts a fourth straight decline and a 5.19% weekly loss as NetEase and Kuaishou crater after earnings, while Alibaba rallies against the tide.
Hang Seng Index Today: Close at 22,410.80, Down 430.82 Points

The Hang Seng Index, the main benchmark of the Hong Kong Stock Exchange, closed Friday, 20 November 2026, at 22,410.80, down 430.82 points or 1.89% from Thursday's close of 22,841.62, according to Hang Seng Indexes data reported by SCMP and Futu. It was the index's lowest close since 30 April 2025, a near 19-month low. During the session it fell as much as 534 points to 22,307.42, which is now its 52-week low.

The Hang Seng Tech Index fell 3.78%, its eighth consecutive daily decline, and briefly broke below the 3,500-point mark. The Hang Seng China Enterprises Index dropped 1.77%. Market turnover reached HK$270.3 billion. Over the week, the Hang Seng Index lost 5.19%, its second straight weekly decline and its fourth losing session in a row.

The sell-off was part of what Asian media called a 'Black Friday' across the region. Anthropic's record initial public offering in New York on Thursday failed to restore faith in the AI trade; US stocks reversed an early rally to close about 2% lower, and the selling spread across Asia overnight. Investors in Hong Kong are particularly focused on whether the enormous investments Chinese platforms are making in data centres and AI models will generate comparable returns.

Additional pressure came from tighter US restrictions on chip exports, including new licensing rules that took effect on Friday for shipments to markets such as Singapore, and from continuing concerns about the Chinese economy. The US dollar strengthened on safe-haven flows, adding to the pressure on Hong Kong assets.

Earnings drove the largest individual moves. NetEase tanked 17.6% and Kuaishou Technology tumbled 11.4% to its lowest level since its 2021 listing after both companies reported disappointing results. Tencent Holdings fell about 1.3% to HK$344, its lowest level in more than two years, after quarterly results showed AI spending weighing on margins. Chipmaker SMIC lost 2.7% to HK$49.12, giving back recent gains and adding to pressure on the technology index.

items.t: Hong Kong Stocks Plunge on "Black Friday": Hang Seng Index Sinks 430 Points for Fourth Straight Loss as NetEase Craters 17% After Earnings
sum: Hong Kong stocks extended their slump on Nov. 20, with the Hang Seng Index opening lower and drifting down to close at 22,410.80, down 430.82 points or 1.89% — its fourth straight daily loss. On a weekly basis, the index fell 5.19%, marking a second consecutive weekly decline. The Hang Seng Tech Index fared worse, closing at 3,511.14, down 138.00 points or 3.78%, while the China Enterprises Index also fell 1.77% to 7,554.37. The market saw broad-based declines, with only 448 stocks advancing against 2,012 decliners, signaling that selling pressure had spread across the board.

The trigger for this correction was a triple whammy: mounting doubts over returns on overseas artificial intelligence investment, strengthening expectations for U.S. rate hikes, and diverging earnings among large technology companies, all of which sharply cooled risk appetite. On the capital-flow front, southbound Stock Connect trading still posted a net inflow of HK$11.812 billion (approximately $1.5 billion) for the day, a contrast against the index's steep drop.

Tech names were the biggest drag on the Nov. 20 session. NetEase, Inc. (9999.HK) plunged 17.60% after reporting third-quarter results, the steepest decline among Hang Seng Tech constituents. The report showed NetEase's total revenue for the quarter was CNY 27.9 billion (approximately $4.2 billion), down 1.8% year over year; non-GAAP net profit attributable to the parent was CNY 9.2 billion (approximately $1.4 billion), down 4% year over year. Revenue from games and related value-added services came in at CNY 22.9 billion (approximately $3.4 billion), down 1.7% year over year, and its market capitalization briefly fell below HK$500 billion (approximately $63.8 billion).

Other tech stocks also came under pressure: Kuaishou (1024.HK) tumbled 11.37%, while Baidu (9888.HK), Xiaomi Group (1810.HK) and Meituan (3690.HK) all closed lower. Tencent Holdings (0700.HK) fell 1.26%, with full-day turnover of HK$14.09 billion (approximately $1.8 billion), the highest in the market.

Hong Kong Stock Exchange: Hang Seng Index Sinks to 22,841.62 Amid Trump, Putin and Xi's Historic Meeting
sum: The Hang Seng Index fell to its lowest level in four months as Tencent slid nearly 7% after weaker-than-expected results and a warning about U.S. chip curbs, while the Hang Seng Tech Index extended its losing streak to seven days.

The Hang Seng Index, the main benchmark of the Hong Kong Stock Exchange, closed at 22,841.62 on Thursday, 19 November 2026, down 453.13 points or 1.95%. The index opened at 23,049.65, which proved to be its high for the day, and fell to an intraday low of 22,772.21 before a modest late recovery. Turnover on the main board was about HK$229.55 billion.

The close is the Hang Seng's lowest in four months and leaves the index just 1.4% above its 52-week low of 22,518.00. It is now down about 18.6% from its 52-week high of 28,056.10, close to bear-market territory, underlining how sharply sentiment toward Hong Kong-listed Chinese technology has deteriorated this autumn.

Tencent Holdings was the biggest single drag on the index. The shares dropped 6.55% to HK$348.40, their lowest level in about 31 months, after the company reported third-quarter revenue growth of around 8%, short of market expectations. Investors were particularly unsettled by Tencent's warning that new U.S. restrictions on advanced chips could slow the training of its artificial intelligence models.

Because Tencent carries one of the largest weightings in the Hang Seng, a drop of that size alone accounts for a significant share of the index's decline. The results also raised questions about the strength of online advertising and consumer spending in China, which weighed on other internet and retail names. Alibaba also fell sharply ahead of its own quarterly results.
How Did the Hang Seng Tech and China Enterprises Indices Perform?

The Hang Seng Tech Index fell 2.33% to 3,649.14, its seventh straight decline and its lowest level in 26 months. The Hang Seng China Enterprises Index, which tracks mainland companies listed in Hong Kong, dropped 1.86% to 7,690.34. The technology gauge's seven-session slide is a clear sign that investors are cutting exposure to Chinese platform and AI names rather than simply taking profits.

items.t: Asia Stocks Split As Tech Wobbles On Fed Rate Signals
sum: Hong Kong’s Hang Seng fell nearly 2% while Japan’s Nikkei 225 ended 0.7% higher.

Asia’s stock markets split on Thursday after US Federal Reserve officials signaled they’re still not done worrying about inflation, and tech shares took the hit. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng slid nearly 2% while Japan’s Nikkei 225 finished 0.7% higher.

When investors think US interest rates may stay high for longer, they tend to value stocks more conservatively. That’s because higher rates raise the “discount rate” – the factor used to translate future profits into today’s dollars – which matters most for growth sectors like technology, where more of the story sits in earnings further out.
That dynamic showed up across Asia-Pacific: the MSCI All Countr..

l Country Asia Pacific Index fell 0.9%, and Taiwan’s TWSE dropped 4.4%, a reminder of how quickly tech-heavy markets can swing when global rate expectations shift. Hong Kong also reflected the more cautious mood, with heavyweight tech-linked names dragging benchmarks lower.
Japan was the outlier. The Nikkei rose 0.7% as company-specific gains offset the global rate jitters, showing that local drivers can still dominate even when the Fed is setting the tone.
For markets: Taiwan’s TWSE fell 4.4% even as the broader Asia-Pacific index slipped 0.9%.

items.t: Asian Markets Split After Nvidia Rally: Nikkei and KOSPI Rise, Hang Seng Falls

In contrast, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng index fell nearly 2% to hit a four-month low, as China tech stocks faced pressure from U.S. chip restrictions.

Nvidia added to the positive mood with its fourth-quarter revenue forecast of around $130 billion, giving semiconductor investors another reason to buy chip stocks.

Hong Kong Stock Exchange: Hang Seng Index Falls to 23,508.17 as Baidu, Alibaba and Tencent Tumble
sum: Hong Kong's benchmark fell for the first time in two sessions on Tuesday as Baidu slid after disappointing results, Alibaba and Tencent tumbled on new US AI chip restrictions, and New World Development plunged after a deeply discounted share sale, even as mainland chipmakers rallied.

The Hang Seng Index closed at 23,508.17 on Tuesday 17 November 2026, down 245.67 points or 1.03% from Monday's close of 23,753.84, according to Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing data reported by The Standard, RTHK and Yahoo Finance. The index opened at 23,521.16, already 232 points lower, and traded between 23,369.32 and 23,626.02 during the session. Turnover on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange rose to HK$198.05 billion.

The Hang Seng Tech Index fell 1.1% to 3,758, while the Hang Seng China Enterprises Index lost around 1%. The decline reversed Monday's modest gain of about 0.7% and left the Hang Seng roughly 9.5% lower than a year earlier, not far above its 52-week low of 22,518.00.

The sell-off followed a sharp decline on Wall Street on Monday, when the Nasdaq Composite fell 2.49% and the S&P 500 dropped 1.92% amid concerns over AI valuations and Nvidia's leadership crisis. Offshore investors, who trade China exposure mainly through Hong Kong, led the selling at the open, when the Hang Seng's decline was more than twice that of the Shanghai market.

Fresh US restrictions on AI chips were the key local catalyst. The US Commerce Department filed an interim final rule requiring licences to ship advanced AI chips to Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and Brazil, and to data centres giving large-scale remote access to Chinese companies. Analysts said the rule could hinder Chinese internet groups' AI ambitions by limiting their access to overseas computing capacity. MT Newswires also cited weaker-than-expected Chinese economic data as a drag on sentiment.

Baidu was among the heaviest decliners, closing down 5.78% at HK$70.90 after reporting quarterly results that highlighted pressure on its advertising revenue despite rapid growth in AI-related businesses. Alibaba fell 5.21% and Tencent lost 3.69%, together accounting for a significant share of the index's decline because of their large weightings. Both Baidu and Alibaba touched fresh lows early in the session.

Asian shares slide on tech weakness ahead of Nvidia earnings
sum: South Korea’s tech-heavy KOSPI slid 2% shortly after the open, while Taiwan stocks fell 1.4%.
Japan’s Nikkei eased 1% and MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan extended early losses to last trade down 1.2%.

Overnight, Washington said it would further restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips from companies like Nvidia. The new rule restricts shipments of advanced chips to data centres like those in Thailand and Malaysia that Chinese companies have used to access computing power to train AI models.

The move came just days after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned following reports of an affair with a woman who worked at Singapore-based cloud company Megaspeed, an Nvidia partner that rents computing power at its data centers. It has come under scrutiny for possible illegal diversion of advanced AI chips to China.

“This is a meaningful escalation because it extends restrictions from physically buying advanced chips to accessing their computing power remotely,” said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo.

“The impact could be significant for providers heavily reliant on Chinese customers training advanced AI models. They could face lower utilisation, weaker pricing and delays to expansion, while licensing uncertainty could make financing new projects harder.”
Markets in China and Hong Kong slid, with the CSI300 blue-chip index down 0.5%, while the Shanghai Composite Index lost 0.65%.

Hong Kong Stocks: Hang Seng Index Closes Up 0.49%, Holds Above 23,700 as Chinese Bank and Consumer Shares Support Market; AI Concept Stocks Slump
sum: On November 16, Hong Kong's three major stock indices moved in different directions. The Hang Seng Index closed up 0.49% at 23,753.84, holding above the 23,700 mark; the China Enterprises Index rose 0.55% to 7,981.54; while the Hang Seng Tech Index bucked the trend and fell 0.30% to close at 3,801.64. Total main board turnover reached HK$174.11 billion (approximately $22.2 billion), with market capital clearly flowing from high-valuation tech sectors into defensive assets such as Chinese bank and consumer stocks.

On the trading floor, Chinese bank stocks and the consumer sector became the main forces supporting the broader market. Benefiting from expectations of a slower pace of net interest margin narrowing in the first three quarters and an increase in dividend payout ratios by large banks, Chinese bank stocks were broadly active, with Industrial and Commercial Bank of China rising more than 2%. Consumer and three-child concept stocks performed notably well, with Haidilao (06682.HK) surging 5.24%, Mengniu Dairy (02319.HK) gaining 4.38%, and Bloks rising more than 7%. Internet sector leaders were generally stronger, with Meituan up 2.51%, and Li Auto and Trip.com rising more than 3% and 2%, respectively.

The warming of the broader consumer sector was not without basis. In dairy products, November is traditionally the off-season for raw milk consumption, but recently the price of loose milk has shown a notable inversion relative to contract milk prices, reflecting an accelerating tightening of upstream raw milk supply. A research report by Guosen Securities noted that under the dual resonance of earlier capacity reduction in reserve dairy cows and the release of downstream deep-processing capacity, raw milk prices are expected to enter a two-to-three-year upward cycle starting in the fourth quarter of 2026.

The restaurant sector has also received fundamental support. Data from China's National Bureau of Statistics showed that national restaurant revenue reached CNY 4.1969 trillion (approximately $630.6 billion) in the first nine months of this year, up 2.4% year-on-year, outpacing total retail sales of consumer goods by about 1.4 percentage points.

sum: AI-linked stocks Zhipu and MiniMax tumbled as Hong Kong extended its recent slide, with the Hang Seng breaking below its key moving averages and losing 844 points over the week despite strong third-quarter GDP data.

The Hang Seng Index closed at 23,637.60 points on Friday 13 November 2026, down 370.95 points or 1.55%, following a 1.26% decline to 24,008.55 on Thursday. The Hang Seng Tech Index fell 3.02% to 3,813.19, while the Hang Seng China Enterprises Index dropped close to 1.5%. Total turnover on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange was about HK$195.8 billion.

The benchmark lost 844 points over the week and closed below all of its major moving averages covering roughly the past six months, a technical breakdown that several local analysts said could lead to further tests of support in the short term. The index opened 0.57% lower, losing the 24,000 level at the outset, and was down 0.92% at 23,786.48 at the midday break before selling intensified in the afternoon.

The dominant story of the session was the abrupt exit of Jensen Huang, the co-founder who had led Nvidia since 1993. The company said on Thursday that he had stepped down as president, chief executive and board member with immediate effect, following reports of multiple affairs, including one with a woman US intelligence suspects of spying for China. Chief financial officer Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO, Harvey C. Jones becomes the company’s first independent chairman, and Nvidia is due to report quarterly results next week. Nvidia shares opened as much as 14% lower on Thursday before closing down 4.34%, and extended losses on Friday after HSBC downgraded the stock.

Hong Kong is home to many of China’s most AI-exposed listed companies, from large-language-model developers to semiconductor foundries and data-centre suppliers, which made it one of the markets most vulnerable to the Nvidia shock. Investors also worried that the combination of Huang’s exit and political change in Washington could slow the pace of US AI infrastructure spending that has supported Asian hardware suppliers.
Geopolitics added a third layer of pressure.

items.t: Как крах акций Nvidia повлияет на паевые инвестиционные фонды США и активы ETF индийских инвесторов
sum: Nvidia’s sharp stock decline has raised concerns among Indian investors holding mutual funds that invest in US equities. However, the impact on most diversified international funds has been relatively limited, with losses ranging between 1% and 3.2%, despite the chipmaker's shares falling 13% in a week.

The bigger risk for Indian investors may lie elsewhere, as some US-focused exchange-traded funds (ETFs) are trading at substantial premiums to the value of their underlying holdings. This exposes buyers to potential losses even if the stocks themselves remain unchanged.
Nvidia shares fell 13% in the week ended November 11. The stock declined another 4.3% the following day after its board opened an inquiry into chief executive Jensen Huang, who subsequently resigned.

For Indian investors, the correction highlights two distinct risks. These include the concentration of individual stocks in mutual fund portfolios and the premiums investors pay when buying overseas ETFs on Indian exchanges.

According to Value Research, most Indian mutual funds investing in US equities lost between 1% and 3.2% during the week ended November 11, considerably less than Nvidia's 13% decline. Three funds even reported positive returns. Mirae Asset NYSE FANG+ ETF FoF gained 7.9%, Motilal Oswal Nasdaq 100 FoF rose 4% and Mirae Asset S&P 500 Top 50 ETF FoF gained 3.2%.

Seven of India's 60 international funds track the Nasdaq 100, making it the most widely tracked overseas index among these schemes. Nvidia accounts for approximately 8% of the index. Therefore, a 13% decline in the stock would translate into an estimated 1% impact on the index, assuming other constituents remain unchanged.
The impact was higher in more concentrated indices. Nvidia accounts for around 10% of the NYSE FANG+ index, which holds just 10 companies, and approximately 12% of the S&P 500 Top 50 index.

The Hang Seng Index, the main benchmark for the Hong Kong Stock Exchange, closed at 24,448.95 on Monday 9 November 2026, down 32.91 points or 0.13% from Friday's close of 24,481.86, according to Hang Seng Indexes Company. The index opened higher at 24,625.71, climbed as much as 257 points to an intraday high of 24,738.88 in the morning, then lost momentum and slipped to a low of 24,421.11 before the close.

The other main gauges also ended lower. The Hang Seng China Enterprises Index, which tracks mainland companies listed in Hong Kong, fell 0.17% to 8,260.15, and the Hang Seng TECH Index dropped 0.92% to 4,040.73. The Hang Seng Composite Index eased 0.08% to 3,521.66, while the Hang Seng Biotech Index was a bright spot, rising 1.41% to 15,056.74.

Hong Kong started the week in line with the rest of Asia, as investors bought technology shares following a late-week recovery on Wall Street. Japan's Nikkei and Taiwan's Taiex surged, but the rally in Hong Kong proved short-lived. Selling pressure built in the afternoon session, with AI-related stocks retreating across the board as investors locked in gains and reassessed the outlook for the sector.

Several factors weighed on sentiment. The weekend announcement that Nvidia's board had opened an investigation into chief executive Jensen Huang, over his relationship with an executive US officials reportedly linked to Chinese intelligence, created fresh uncertainty around US-China technology ties, even though Beijing dismissed the allegations. Investors were also cautious ahead of quarterly results from Tencent, Baidu and Lenovo, which will provide an important read on Chinese AI spending, and after official data showed mainland consumer inflation slowed in October.

Food delivery giant Meituan was the heaviest drag among the large caps, dropping more than 6% in a market already wary of the intense price competition in China's instant retail and delivery sector, which has pressured the group's profitability for much of the past year.

sum: Alibaba's stock closed Friday with a 2.0% gain, a move that landed alongside a broader rebound in AI-linked equities following a two-day selloff. The advance came as the company's leadership used a high-profile platform to make the case for open-source artificial intelligence — while conceding that the hardware to run it is in short supply.

Chairman Joe Tsai, speaking Tuesday at the World Internet Conference Wuzhen Summit, touted the merits of open AI models and flagged bottlenecks in computing capacity as demand climbs, according to media reports. His remarks sketch both the promise and the pressure point for investors weighing whether Alibaba's AI buildout can pay for itself.

The Friday uptick was part of a wider recovery in technology names. AP reported a bounce after the two-day rout but drew no explicit link to Alibaba's own share movement. A day earlier, the stock had already ridden a broad rally in Hong Kong tech stocks: Reuters reported the Hang Seng Tech Index climbed 5%, with the agency pointing to improved market sentiment after the US midterm elections and tech names leading the gains.

Earlier in the week, media coverage tied rising Chinese equities to reports of planned central bank discussions on stronger credit support for share buybacks and stake increases. Alibaba was named among the beneficiaries; no additional financing was reported as having been agreed. Coverage also cited the planned integration of Alibaba's Qwen model into Apple's offering for the Chinese market — a December consumer launch of Apple Intelligence using the Alibaba model that was reported roughly a week ago.

The strategic logic Tsai outlined rests on a simple linkage: open models only generate value if there is enough infrastructure to serve them. That connection between technology and compute capacity is where Alibaba's approach will ultimately be judged.

The central question for investors is whether the company can convert growing AI usage into economically viable business. Supporting the bullish reading, Alibaba has already announced concrete deployments of its technology. The most telling evidence going forward would be signs that those deployments generate additional demand for Alibaba's cloud and AI services — and that the demand translates into revenue.

China’s blue-chip CSI 300 Index dropped 1.4 percent, but notched up a 1.7 percent gain for the week to snap a 12-week-long losing streak.
The Shanghai Composite Index fell 1.1 percent on Friday, though it ended the week 1.4 percent higher, breaking a six-week run of declines.

In Hong Kong, the benchmark Hang Seng Index was down 1.3 percent but registered a 5.1 percent weekly gain, its best since March 2025. The Hang Seng Tech Index slid 1.8 percent on Friday, but posted its best weekly gain since February 2025, advancing 8.6 percent.

Tech sectors across Asia took a heavy blow after a steep selloff overnight in the US wiped trillions of dollars off market value, as investors fretted that a Democratic sweep in the US midterm elections could bring tighter scrutiny of the AI sector.
China’s tech-focused Star 50 Index and the AI Index slumped as much as 5.2 percent before paring some losses.
Dong Baozhen, chairman of asset manager Lingtong Shengtai, said the overnight slump in US tech stocks meant the logic behind the AI-driven rally had crumbled.

sum: Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index rose 0.42% to 23,393.32 on Monday 2 November 2026, its second straight gain, as the Hang Seng Tech Index surged 2.25% led by Xiaomi, CATL, Alibaba and Tencent, while banks and gold miners lagged.

The Hang Seng Index, the main benchmark of the Hong Kong Stock Exchange, closed at 23,393.32 on Monday, up 98.90 points or 0.42%, according to Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing data reported by Xinhua and The Standard. It followed Friday's 1.5% rebound and marked the index's first session of November in positive territory.

The index traded as high as 23,543.30 but gave back part of those gains in the afternoon. The more significant move came in technology: the Hang Seng Tech Index jumped 2.25% to 3,839.41 after rising as much as 3% intraday, while the Hang Seng China Enterprises Index added 0.56% to 7,906.11. Full-day turnover reached HK$204.84 billion.

Two forces supported the market. First, expectations of fresh policy support in mainland China lifted sentiment, after regulators met banks and brokers to discuss stabilising the equity market and the People's Bank of China signalled a new liquidity operation. Chinese brokerage stocks were among the leaders as investors bet on higher trading volumes.

Second, easing oil prices and a recovery in US stock futures after Friday's technology sell-off gave investors confidence to buy back into beaten-down tech names ahead of Apple's quarterly results. Even so, the gain in the broader Hang Seng was modest because banks and gold-related stocks, which had served as havens in October, were sold to fund purchases elsewhere.

Xiaomi was the best-performing blue chip, rising 6.1%, followed closely by battery giant CATL, which gained about 6% as lithium battery shares rallied. Among the heavyweights, Alibaba climbed 2.5% and Tencent advanced 2.2%, together providing a large share of the index's points gain.

Chipmakers also recovered. Hua Hong Semiconductor rose nearly 3% and SMIC added 1.5%. Casino operators climbed despite a decline in Macao's October gaming revenue, with Galaxy Entertainment up 3.7% and Sands China up 3.1%. On the downside, Bank of China and BOC Hong Kong were among the weakest constituents after their recent results, and gold miners eased.

sum: Weekly Review: Examining the "rewarded mistake" through the lens of southbound funds in Hong Kong stocks.

Close on Oct 30,$Hang Seng Index (800000.HK)$ at 23,294.42 points, up 0.87% for the week, ending two consecutive weeks of declines; $Hang Seng TECH Index (800700.HK)$ at 3,754.90 points, down 3.02% for the week; the SOE Index rose 1.37% for the week.

But what is truly glaring is not the indices, but the capital flows: Southbound funds recorded net sales of HKD 3.56 billion on Oct 30. This marks the 13th consecutive trading day of net selling, setting a new record for the longest streak of continuous net outflows, with cumulative outflows totaling HKD 37.323 billion over the 13-day period.Net outflows for the entire month of October approached HKD 28 billion, the largest single-month figure since July 2021.
Money is flowing out on one side, while indices are rising on the other.

The structural divergence is also stark: On Oct 30, consumer and energy sectors led the gains— $MAO GEPING (01318.HK)$ up over 13%, $MENGNIU DAIRY (02319.HK)$ up over 9%, $SINOPEC CORP (00386.HK)$ up 6.22%, $PETROCHINA (00857.HK)$ up 5.66%; meanwhile, the semiconductor sector continues to face pressure,$SMIC (00981.HK)$ down over 4%, $GIGADEVICE (03986.HK)$ down more than 8%. Looking at the full week,$SMIC (00981.HK)$ Down 8.67%, with southbound capital withdrawing approximately RMB 4.1 billion from it over the past seven days.
[But what is most worth pondering is this month's "rebound"]
The Hang Seng TECH Index fell 11.73% in October, declining steadily. Throughout this process, almost every minor rebound was beaten back by selling pressure.
items.to: Southbound capital withdrew for a record 13 consecutive days, yet the Hang Seng Index rose instead—this market keeps rewarding a mistake.
